rules.statement: In logout handling, never read or reverse the `sub` claim of an `id_token_hint`. Take only its `sid` and client (`azp`/`aud`), and resolve the stable subject and the participating clients from server-owned state: the persisted session grant matched forward by `sid`, or the login cookie.
rules.why: For a pairwise client, the hint's `sub` is a per-sector pseudonym. It matches no grant and no relying party, and reversing it would need a reversible map that a store compromise could use to de-anonymize users.
rules.check: Look for logout or end-session code that reads `sub` from the hint and uses it for revocation, session lookup or back-channel fan-out.

rules.statement: Don't add a stored, reversible mapping (table, entity or cache) from a pairwise subject identifier back to the principal. Match pairwise values forward by projecting the principal instead.
rules.why: A reversible map is a standing de-anonymization liability: one store compromise re-links every pairwise `sub`. It also contradicts the system's one-way posture.
rules.check: Look for new persistence or lookups keyed by a pairwise `sub` that return a principal id.

rules.statement: An OpenID Connect end-session endpoint must ask the end user to confirm whenever an OP login is present and the request carries no valid `id_token_hint` whose `sid` ordinally equals the login's `sid`. It must not sign the user out unprompted in that case.
rules.why: OpenID Connect RP-Initiated Logout 1.0 section 2 requires the prompt, and it closes logout CSRF from cross-site links and forms.
rules.check: Check end-session changes for a path that ends the session without a matching-`sid` hint and without confirmation, and for `sid` comparisons that are not ordinal.

rules.statement: When an OP login is present during logout, the session to end comes from the login's `sid`, not the hint's. Use the hint's `sid` only when no login is present.
rules.why: A confirmed logout must end the session the end user is actually signed in to, so a validly signed hint can't steer the logout to a different session or subject.
rules.check: Look at session resolution in logout code for a hint `sid` that overrides the authenticated login's `sid`.

rules.statement: Implement logout confirmation through a one-time, unguessable continuation URL that the server keeps. Never use a 'confirmed' flag or parameter posted back to the endpoint.
rules.why: Anyone can forge a posted confirmation flag. The one-time continuation's unguessable state acts as the CSRF secret.
rules.check: Look for confirmation logic that trusts a request parameter such as `confirmed=true` instead of redeeming a server-held continuation.

rules.statement: When resuming a parked logout continuation, resolve the current session again and refuse with `invalid_request` when its session id differs from the parked one. Treat the continuation as spent and send nothing to the relying party.
rules.why: Otherwise a continuation obtained in one browser could end another browser's session.
rules.check: Look for continue or resume handlers that proceed without comparing the parked session id with the current one.

rules.statement: When a logout resolved no subject and no session (no login was seen), don't call `SignOutAsync` and don't clear browser state in the response.
rules.why: A cross-site POST doesn't carry the `SameSite=Lax` login cookie, so its response must not be able to clear the login through `Set-Cookie`.
rules.check: Look for logout handlers that sign out or clear cookies unconditionally, even when no subject or session was resolved.

rules.statement: Redirect after logout only to a `post_logout_redirect_uri` that ordinally and exactly matches one of the client's registered `post_logout_redirect_uris` and passes the redirect-URI kind check. Otherwise render a confirmation page and don't redirect.
rules.why: Exact matching against the registered URIs prevents open redirects from the end-session endpoint.
rules.check: Look for redirect URI comparisons in logout code that are case-insensitive, prefix-based or normalized, or that redirect when no registered URI matches.

rules.statement: Make a back-channel `logout_token` a signed JWT with `typ` `logout+jwt` and the claims `iss`, `aud`, `iat`, `jti`, `events` and `sid` and/or `sub`. Project `sub` per receiving client so it matches the `sub` that client saw in its ID token.
rules.why: Back-Channel Logout 1.0 defines this token. A pairwise relying party only recognizes the `sub` projected for its own sector.
rules.check: Look for logout tokens that are missing `typ` or required claims, or that reuse one `sub` across all clients instead of projecting it per client.

rules.statement: Back-channel logout must follow the tenant's discovery metadata. Send nothing while `backchannel_logout_supported` is false, and omit `sid` while `backchannel_logout_session_supported` is false.
rules.why: The OP must not behave differently from what its discovery document advertises.
rules.check: Look for notifier code that sends logout tokens or includes `sid` without checking the corresponding discovery setting.

rules.statement: Deliver back-channel logout notifications to relying parties out of band through a deferred job dispatcher, not inline in the logout request.
rules.why: A failed delivery can then be retried out of band, and the notification doesn't depend on the browser.
rules.check: Look for logout code that makes HTTP calls to `backchannel_logout_uri` directly inside the request pipeline.

rules.statement: Make a security-relevant decision on a replaceable handler's result type (such as whether confirmation is required) a positional record member, so every replacement handler has to state it explicitly in order to compile.
rules.why: A defaulted or optional member would let a replacement handler silently pick the insecure behavior, for example logging out without a prompt.
rules.check: Look for security-decision properties on extensible result records that are optional, have defaults or are init-only rather than positional.

rules.statement: When logging a refused or mismatched session continuation, don't include the session id or the continuation URL or state in the log.
rules.why: Session identifiers and one-time continuation secrets are credentials, and logs must not leak them.
rules.check: Look for log messages in session or continuation code that interpolate session ids, continue URLs or `state` values.
